lessons.title: Compare ways to write numbers
ideas: An additive numeral adds the values of its symbols.
A positional numeral uses both a symbol and its location.
We can compare systems without claiming one historical method works exactly like another.

Egyptian numerals used repeated powers-of-ten symbols; Roman notation also uses subtractive pairs such as IV. Babylonian place value grouped in base 60; Mayan positional notation commonly grouped in base 20 and used a zero sign. Indian decimal positional notation made ten-place grouping and zero especially powerful. These systems developed over long periods and have different conventions.

lessons.title: Rectangles, rhombi and squares
ideas: A rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles.

A kite has two pairs of adjacent equal sides. Its diagonal through the vertices between equal-side pairs is a symmetry axis in a non-rhombus kite.

ideas: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side.
The square areas on the two shorter sides add to the square area on the hypotenuse.
The theorem applies to right triangles, not all triangles.

ideas: Square first, then add or subtract, then take a root.

lessons.title: Repeated rules make fractals
ideas: A fractal repeats a structure at different scales.
At every Sierpinski triangle step, keep three of four equal smaller triangles.

examples.question: How many triangles are kept after $4$ Sierpinski steps?
steps: Each step multiplies the count by $3$: $3^4$.

examples.question: A triangle has area $128\text{ cm}^2$. Find the area kept after $3$ Sierpinski steps.

experiment.title: Hands-on: repeated rules make fractals
steps: Draw a triangle and join side midpoints.
Remove the central triangle; repeat on the three corner triangles.
experiment.result: The number of kept triangles triples while total area is multiplied by three quarters.

lessons.title: Nets fold into solids
ideas: A net is a connected arrangement of faces that folds without overlaps.
A cube has six square faces, twelve edges and eight vertices.
Not every six-square arrangement is a cube net.

examples.question: Check Euler's formula $F+V-E=2$ for a square pyramid.
A net has $2$ triangles and $3$ rectangles. Name the solid and find $F$, $E$, $V$.
steps: It folds into a triangular prism.

examples.question: A cross-shaped cube net has a row of four squares P, Q, R, S, with T above Q and U below Q. Which faces are opposite?
steps: In the row, faces two apart are opposite.
T and U are on opposite sides of Q.

experiment.title: Hands-on: nets fold into solids
steps: Cut a six-square cross net with tabs.
Fold and test whether every face meets correctly.
experiment.result: A real fold is a useful check for overlap and missing faces.

lessons.title: Views and isometric drawings
ideas: Top, front and side views show different information.
A hidden cube may appear in one view but not another.
An isometric drawing represents three directions with a consistent scale; apparent angles are not measured solid angles.

examples.question: A one-cube-deep stack has columns of heights $2,1,3$. Find the number of cubes and describe its front view.
steps: Front view shows columns of heights $2,1,3$.

examples.question: How many unit cubes make a $3\times2\times1$ cuboid?
Four cubes form a $2\times2$ square layer and one cube sits on a corner. Find the count and the top view.
steps: From above we see a $2\times2$ square.

experiment.title: Hands-on: views and isometric drawings
steps: Build a stack of unit cubes.
Draw its top, front and right views.
experiment.result: More than one stack can sometimes share the same views.

lessons.title: Find a shortest path on a surface
ideas: A straight line is shortest in an unfolded plane.
Try valid unfoldings, then compare their straight-line lengths.
The shortest surface route is not usually a space diagonal through the solid.

examples.question: An ant walks on the surface of a $2\times3\times6$ cuboid between opposite corners. Find the shortest route.
Compare that route with the straight line through the inside of the same cuboid.
steps: $7<7.81$, but the ant cannot pass through the solid.

experiment.title: Hands-on: find a shortest path on a surface
steps: Flatten two adjacent rectangular faces of a box.
Draw a straight route between opposite corners.
experiment.result: Refolding gives a straight-on-the-net route along the surface.

lessons.title: The mean is a balance point
ideas: The mean shares a total equally among observations.
A large value pulls the mean toward it.
The mean need not be one of the observations.

examples.question: Find the mean of $12,15,18,21,24$.

experiment.title: Hands-on: the mean is a balance point
steps: Place equal counters at data values on a number line.
Move the balance point until the signed distances add to zero.
experiment.result: That point is the mean.

lessons.title: How changes affect averages
ideas: Adding a value above the current mean raises the mean.
Removing a below-mean value also raises the mean.
Adding the same number to every observation increases the mean by that number.

examples.question: The mean of $8$ numbers is $20$. The number $34$ is removed. Find the new mean.

steps: The total doubles and the count stays the same.

experiment.title: Hands-on: how changes affect averages
experiment.result: The total and the count both change; recompute rather than averaging the two means.

lessons.title: Median and sensible comparisons
ideas: Sort the data before finding a median.

experiment.title: Hands-on: median and sensible comparisons

lessons.title: Rational numbers and density
ideas: A rational number is an integer divided by a non-zero integer.
There is no next rational number: their average lies between any two different rational numbers.
Decimals of rational numbers terminate or eventually repeat.

examples.question: Find three rational numbers between $\dfrac25$ and $\dfrac35$.
Express $0.\overline{6}$ and $1.\overline{27}$ as fractions.

steps: $16=2^4$: only the prime $2$, so it terminates.

experiment.title: Hands-on: rational numbers and density
steps: Mark one half and three quarters on a number line.
experiment.result: You can repeat the averaging process forever to create more rational numbers.

lessons.title: Irrational numbers
ideas: An irrational number cannot be expressed as an integer ratio.
Its decimal neither terminates nor eventually repeats.
A decimal that merely looks long is not automatically irrational.

examples.question: Classify $\sqrt{16}$, $\sqrt{12}$, $0.1010010001\ldots$ and $\dfrac{22}7$ as rational or irrational.
steps: The decimal never repeats a block, so it is irrational. $\dfrac{22}7$ is a ratio of integers.

lessons.title: Prove irrationality
ideas: A contradiction proof assumes the opposite in a precise form.
Write the supposed fraction in lowest terms.

steps: Suppose $\sqrt5=\dfrac pq$ in lowest terms. Then $p^2=5q^2$, so $5$ divides $p$.
$p$ and $q$ share the factor $5$, which contradicts lowest terms.

steps: If it were rational, $\sqrt7=\dfrac72\times$ (that number) would be rational.

lessons.title: Euclid’s first four postulates
ideas: A straight segment can join any two points.
A segment can be extended indefinitely; a circle can be drawn with any centre and positive radius.
All right angles are equal.

examples.question: State Euclid's fourth postulate and explain its use.
steps: All right angles are equal to one another.

examples.question: How many lines pass through one point? Through two distinct points?
steps: Exactly one through two distinct points.

steps: Mark two distinct points and join them.

In Euclidean geometry an equivalent statement gives one parallel through a point outside a line.

examples.question: State Playfair's axiom.
steps: It is equivalent to Euclid's fifth postulate.
examples.result: Through a point not on a line, exactly one line is parallel to it.

steps: If $l$ and $m$ met at a point, two parallels to $n$ would pass through it.

examples.question: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB>AC$. Which of $\angle B$ and $\angle C$ is larger?

examples.question: Can $4$ cm, $5$ cm and $10$ cm form a triangle?
In right $\triangle ABC$ with $\angle C=90^\circ$, M is the midpoint of $AB$. Extend CM to D with $MD=CM$. Prove $CM=\tfrac12AB$.

g9-quadrilaterals.title: 4-gons (Quadrilaterals)
g9-quadrilaterals.subtitle: CBSE Mathematics 2026–27 · Start from basics; build confidence one step at a time

lessons.title: Parallelogram properties and their converses
ideas: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are parallel and equal.
Opposite angles are equal; adjacent angles sum to 180 degrees.
Diagonals bisect each other; equal diagonals are a special rectangle property.

examples.question: In parallelogram ABCD, $\angle A=3x+10$ and $\angle B=2x$. Find all angles.
Show that a quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other is a parallelogram.
steps: With $OA=OC$, $OB=OD$ and vertical angles, $\triangle AOB\cong\triangle COD$ (SAS).
So $\angle OAB=\angle OCD$: alternate angles, $AB\parallel CD$. Similarly $AD\parallel BC$.

examples.question: Show that the diagonals of a rectangle are equal.
steps: $\triangle ABC\cong\triangle DCB$: $AB=DC$, $BC$ common, right angles at $B$ and $C$ (SAS).

experiment.title: Hands-on: parallelogram properties and their converses
steps: Cut a parallelogram along a diagonal.
Match triangles using parallel-angle facts and the common diagonal.
experiment.result: Congruence explains equal opposite sides.

lessons.title: The midpoint theorem
ideas: The segment joining midpoints of two triangle sides is parallel to the third side.
Its length is half the third side.
The converse lets a parallel through one midpoint identify the other midpoint.

examples.question: In $\triangle PQR$, $S$ and $T$ are midpoints of $PQ$ and $PR$. $ST=7.5$ cm. Find $QR$.
The sides of a triangle are $8$, $10$ and $12$ cm. Find the perimeter of the triangle formed by joining the midpoints.
steps: Each new side is half a side of the original.

examples.question: In $\triangle ABC$, $D$ is the midpoint of $AB$. A line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ meets $AC$ at $E$. $AC=9$ cm. Find $AE$.
steps: The converse of the midpoint theorem: $E$ is the midpoint of $AC$.

experiment.title: Hands-on: the midpoint theorem
steps: Mark side midpoints on a paper triangle.
Join them and compare with the third side.
experiment.result: Measure to conjecture, then prove using a parallelogram construction.

lessons.title: Medians, centroids and central symmetry
ideas: A median joins a vertex to the opposite side’s midpoint.
The three medians meet at the centroid, which divides each in ratio 2:1 from the vertex.
A parallelogram has half-turn symmetry about the diagonal intersection.

examples.question: G is the centroid of $\triangle ABC$ and $AG=8$ cm. Find the median $AD$.
Find the centroid of the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(6,0)$ and $(3,9)$.
Does a rhombus have half-turn symmetry? About which point?
steps: Every parallelogram does, about the point where the diagonals meet.
examples.result: Yes, about the meeting point of its diagonals

experiment.title: Hands-on: medians, centroids and central symmetry
steps: Cut a uniform triangle from card and draw its medians.
experiment.result: The balance suggests why the centroid matters; the 2:1 ratio needs a geometric proof.

lessons.title: Midpoint quadrilaterals and tiling
ideas: Joining side midpoints of any simple quadrilateral produces a parallelogram.
The midpoint theorem makes opposite sides parallel to the same diagonal.
Half-turn copies of a quadrilateral can form a plane tiling without gaps.

examples.question: For parallelogram ABCD shown with $\angle A=110^\circ$, $AC=16$ and $BD=10$, find $\angle C$, $AO$ and $OD$.
Joining the midpoints of a rectangle's sides gives which shape? Why?
steps: The midpoint figure has sides half of each diagonal.
The diagonals of a rectangle are equal, so all four sides are equal.

examples.question: Joining the midpoints of a rhombus's sides gives which shape? Why?
steps: Its sides are parallel to the diagonals.
The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular, so the angles are right angles.

experiment.title: Hands-on: midpoint quadrilaterals and tiling
steps: Join the four side midpoints of a quadrilateral.
experiment.result: Two midpoint segments are each parallel to one original diagonal, so opposite sides are parallel.

diagram.caption: ABCD is a parallelogram with angle A=110°; its diagonals meet at O.

ideas: Read the question twice and decide which idea it tests.
Write each step with a reason; check the answer in the original question.
These questions mix ideas from the whole chapter.

examples.question: In trapezium ABCD, $AB\parallel DC$, $AB=14$ cm and $DC=8$ cm. Find the segment joining the midpoints of $AD$ and $BC$.
steps: Join $AC$; use the midpoint theorem in $\triangle ADC$ and $\triangle CAB$.

examples.question: Prove that the angle bisectors of a parallelogram form a rectangle.
steps: Two adjacent bisectors meet at $\tfrac12(\angle A+\angle B)=90^\circ$.
All four angles of the new figure are right angles.

examples.question: ABCD is a square and $P$ is a point on $BD$. Prove $AP=CP$.

g9-circles.title: Circles
g9-circles.subtitle: CBSE Mathematics 2026–27 · Start from basics; build confidence one step at a time

lessons.title: Centre, radius, chord and diameter
ideas: A circle is the set of points at a fixed distance from a centre.
A chord joins two boundary points; a diameter is a chord through the centre.
The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects that chord.

examples.question: In the circle shown, $r=13$ cm and the chord is $5$ cm from the centre. Find the chord.
A chord of length $16$ cm is $6$ cm from the centre. Find the radius.
Two parallel chords of lengths $6$ cm and $8$ cm lie on opposite sides of the centre of a circle of radius $5$ cm. Find the distance between them.

experiment.title: Hands-on: centre, radius, chord and diameter
steps: Draw a chord on a paper circle.
Fold through the centre perpendicular to the chord.
experiment.result: Its two halves meet.

diagram.caption: A circle has radius 13 units; the chord AB is 5 units from the centre O.

lessons.title: Equal chords and circumcircles
ideas: Equal chords of the same or congruent circles have equal distances from their centres.
The perpendicular bisectors of a triangle sides meet at its circumcentre.
A non-collinear triple has a unique circumcircle.

examples.question: Chords AB and CD are equal and $OM\perp AB$ with $OM=4$ cm. Find the distance of CD from O.
steps: Equal chords are equidistant from the centre.

examples.question: Where is the circumcentre of a right triangle?
steps: The hypotenuse subtends $90^\circ$, so it is a diameter.

examples.question: How many circles pass through three collinear points? Through three non-collinear points?
steps: Perpendicular bisectors of collinear segments are parallel and never meet.
For a triangle they meet at one point.

experiment.title: Hands-on: equal chords and circumcircles
steps: Draw a triangle and construct two side perpendicular bisectors.
experiment.result: It is equally distant from all three vertices.

lessons.title: Angles on the same arc
ideas: An angle at the centre is twice an angle at the circumference subtending the same arc.
Angles in the same segment are equal.
An angle in a semicircle is right; distinguish the arc under consideration.

examples.question: $\angle ACB=48^\circ$ on arc AB. Find the central angle $\angle AOB$.
C and D lie on the same arc of chord AB. $\angle ACB=40^\circ$. Find $\angle ADB$.
steps: Angles in the same segment are equal.

examples.question: $AB$ is a diameter and $\angle CAB=28^\circ$. Find $\angle ABC$.

experiment.title: Hands-on: angles on the same arc
steps: Keep chord endpoints fixed and move a third point around one arc.
Measure the angle at that point.
experiment.result: Within the same segment it stays constant.

lessons.title: Cyclic quadrilaterals
ideas: A cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on one circle.
Its opposite angles are supplementary.
The converse lets a180-degree opposite-angle sum prove cyclicity for a convex quadrilateral.

examples.question: ABCD is cyclic with $\angle B=3x$ and $\angle D=2x+30$. Find $x$.
ABCD is cyclic. $\angle DAB=95^\circ$ and the side $BC$ is extended to E. Find $\angle DCE$.
examples.result: $95^\circ$ (the exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle)

examples.question: Is every rectangle cyclic? Is every rhombus?
steps: A non-square rhombus has unequal opposite-angle sums.
examples.result: Rectangle yes; rhombus only if it is a square

experiment.title: Hands-on: cyclic quadrilaterals
steps: Measure one pair of opposite angles.
experiment.result: Their sum is 180 degrees even when you move a vertex along the circle.

lessons.title: Higher-order practice
ideas: Read the question twice and decide which idea it tests.
Write each step with a reason; check the answer in the original question.
These questions mix ideas from the whole chapter.

examples.question: A chord of a circle equals its radius. Find the angle it subtends at a point on the major arc.
steps: The chord and two radii form an equilateral triangle: centre angle $60^\circ$.

examples.question: Prove that a cyclic parallelogram is a rectangle.
steps: Opposite angles are equal (parallelogram) and add to $180^\circ$ (cyclic).

examples.question: Two circles of radii $5$ cm and $3$ cm meet at two points. Their centres are $4$ cm apart. Find the common chord.
steps: $3^2+4^2=5^2$, so the chord passes through the smaller centre and is a diameter of the small circle.

g9-area-perimeter.title: Area and Perimeter
g9-area-perimeter.subtitle: CBSE Mathematics 2026–27 · Start from basics; build confidence one step at a time

lessons.title: Separate boundary from surface
ideas: Perimeter measures a boundary in length units.
Area measures coverage in square units.
A triangle needs perpendicular height; a sloping side is not the height unless perpendicular.

examples.question: A square and a rectangle $16$ m by $9$ m have equal area. Compare their perimeters.
steps: Area $=144$, so the square's side $=12$: perimeter $48$.

examples.question: Find the cost of fencing a $25\times18$ m field at ₹$40$ per metre.
A triangle has base $18$ cm and area $108\text{ cm}^2$. Find its height.

experiment.title: Hands-on: separate boundary from surface
steps: Build rectangles with the same perimeter but different sides.
experiment.result: Equal perimeter does not force equal area.

lessons.title: Heron’s formula
ideas: Heron finds triangle area when all three sides are known.
Check triangle inequality before using the formula.
The semiperimeter is half the perimeter; keep exact roots until the end.

examples.question: Use Heron's formula for the triangle shown, with sides $9$, $10$ and $17$ cm.
Find the area of a triangle with sides $10$, $10$ and $12$ cm.
A triangle has perimeter $42$ cm and sides in the ratio $3:4:5$. Find its area.

experiment.title: Hands-on: heron’s formula
experiment.result: Heron gives 84 square units; the altitude to base 14 is 12.

diagram.caption: A triangle has sides 9 cm, 10 cm and 17 cm.

lessons.title: Brahmagupta for cyclic quadrilaterals
ideas: The square-root formula below requires a cyclic quadrilateral.
A general quadrilateral with the same four sides can have a different area.
Verify the cyclic condition rather than assuming it from a sketch.

examples.question: Find the area of a cyclic quadrilateral with sides $5$, $5$, $5$ and $5$ cm.
steps: A cyclic rhombus is a square.

examples.question: A cyclic quadrilateral has sides $6$, $8$, $6$, $8$ m. Find its area.
Find the area of quadrilateral ABCD with $AB=9$, $BC=12$, $CD=8$, $DA=17$ and diagonal $AC=15$, using two triangles.

experiment.title: Hands-on: brahmagupta for cyclic quadrilaterals
steps: Use a rectangular card with sides 3 and 4.
Its four vertices lie on a circle.
experiment.result: The formula gives the familiar rectangle area 12.

lessons.title: Sectors, segments and composite regions
ideas: A sector is a wedge bounded by radii and an arc.
A segment is the region between a chord and its arc.
Segment area equals sector area minus the appropriate triangle area.

examples.question: Find the area and arc of a sector of radius $14$ cm and angle $45^\circ$ ($\pi=\tfrac{22}7$).
Find the perimeter of a semicircular plate of radius $21$ cm ($\pi=\tfrac{22}7$).
A square of side $14$ cm has a quarter circle of radius $14$ cm drawn from one corner. Find the area outside the quarter circle.

experiment.title: Hands-on: sectors, segments and composite regions
steps: Draw a90-degree sector and its connecting chord.
Shade the triangle and the leftover segment separately.
experiment.result: Adding their areas recovers the sector.

ideas: Read the question twice and decide which idea it tests.
Write each step with a reason; check the answer in the original question.
These questions mix ideas from the whole chapter.

Find the area of a minor segment of a circle of radius $6$ cm with central angle $60^\circ$.
Show that Heron's formula gives $\tfrac{\sqrt3}4a^2$ for an equilateral triangle of side $a$.

CSA_{\rm cone}=\pi rl,\quad V_{\rm cone}=\frac13\pi r^2h

lessons.title: Nets, exposed faces and capacity
ideas: Surface area measures exposed covering; volume measures occupied space.
A net helps you avoid counting hidden or missing faces.
Keep all lengths in one unit before squaring or cubing.

examples.question: Find the total surface area of a cuboid $10\times6\times4$ cm.
A cube has total surface area $150\text{ cm}^2$. Find its volume.
An open box is $50\times40\times30$ cm. How much sheet is needed (no lid)?

experiment.title: Hands-on: nets, exposed faces and capacity
experiment.result: Adding all six face areas gives the total surface area.

lessons.title: Cylinders and cones
ideas: A cylinder curved surface unfolds to a rectangle.
A cone uses slant height for curved area, but vertical height for volume.
A cone has one third the volume of a cylinder with the same base and height.
formulas: CSA_{\rm cyl}=2\pi rh,\quad V_{\rm cyl}=\pi r^2h
CSA_{\rm cone}=\pi rl,\quad V_{\rm cone}=\frac13\pi r^2h

examples.question: For the cylinder shown ($r=14$ cm, $h=20$ cm), find the curved surface area and volume ($\pi=\tfrac{22}7$).
A cone has radius $7$ cm and slant height $25$ cm. Find its height and volume.
A conical tent has radius $6$ m and height $8$ m. Find the canvas needed.

experiment.title: Hands-on: cylinders and cones
steps: Fill a cone and pour into a same-base same-height cylinder.
experiment.result: Three cone volumes fill the cylinder; wet-lab measurements only approximate the mathematical ratio.

diagram.caption: A closed cylinder has radius 14 cm and height 20 cm.

lessons.title: Spheres, hemispheres and pyramids
ideas: A sphere surface has no flat face.
A hemisphere total area includes its circular base.
A pyramid volume is one third base area times perpendicular height; sloping faces need their own heights.

examples.question: Find the surface area of a sphere of radius $7$ cm ($\pi=\tfrac{22}7$).
A hemispherical bowl has radius $21$ cm. Find its capacity in litres.
A square pyramid has base $10$ m and height $12$ m. Find the slant height and the total surface area.

experiment.title: Hands-on: spheres, hemispheres and pyramids
steps: Compare a hemisphere bowl with its circular lid.
Distinguish the curved bowl surface from the lid.
experiment.result: Total external surface includes both if the solid is closed.

lessons.title: Recasting, scale and litres
ideas: Recasting preserves volume when no material is lost.
Doubling lengths multiplies area by 4 and volume by 8.
Capacity uses internal dimensions; one litre is 1000 cubic centimetres.

examples.question: A cylinder of radius $3$ cm and height $16$ cm is melted into spheres of radius $2$ cm. How many spheres?
The radius of a sphere is doubled. How do its surface area and volume change?
A tank $2\text{ m}\times1.5\text{ m}\times1$ m is filled by a pipe at $50$ L per minute. How long does it take?

experiment.title: Hands-on: recasting, scale and litres
steps: Make cubes of edge 1 and 2 using unit blocks.
Compare face squares and block counts.
experiment.result: Area grows from 6 to 24 while volume grows from 1 to 8.

Write each step with a reason; check the answer in the original question.
These questions mix ideas from the whole chapter.

examples.question: A cone and a cylinder have the same base and the same height. The cylinder holds $1.5$ L. How much does the cone hold?

g9-statistics.title: Statistics
g9-statistics.subtitle: CBSE Mathematics 2026–27 · Start from basics; build confidence one step at a time

lessons.title: Read and organise data
ideas: A frequency counts how often a value or category occurs.
Check axis labels, units and total sample size before comparing graphs.
A bar graph uses separated categories; a histogram represents contiguous numerical intervals.

examples.question: From the bar chart shown (frequencies $6,9,4,11$), find the total and the share of the largest category.
When is a histogram used instead of a bar graph?
steps: For numerical data grouped in touching class intervals.

experiment.title: Hands-on: read and organise data
steps: Survey ten classmates about a category.
experiment.result: Frequencies should add to ten.

diagram.caption: Four categories have frequencies 6, 9, 4 and 11 on a common scale.

lessons.title: Mean, median and mode
ideas: The mean uses every value.
The median is the middle of sorted observations.
The mode is a most frequent value; there may be more than one or no unique mode.

examples.question: Find the mean of $15,22,18,30,25$.
Find the median of $34,28,41,30,36,29$.
Find the mode of $4,7,7,2,9,4,7,5$.

experiment.title: Hands-on: mean, median and mode
steps: Find total 20, middle 3 and most frequent 3.
experiment.result: Mean 4,median 3,mode 3 describe different features.

lessons.title: Weighted averages
ideas: A combined average must account for group sizes.
Multiply each group average by its count to recover its total.
For arbitrary group means, directly averaging them is guaranteed correct when group sizes are equal. Otherwise use weights; identical group means are a special case.

examples.question: $25$ boys average $40$ kg and $15$ girls average $36$ kg. Find the mean weight of the class.
Marks $10,20,30,40$ have frequencies $2,5,8,5$. Find the mean.
A test has weights: theory $60\%$, practical $40\%$. Riya scores $70$ and $90$. Find her weighted score.

experiment.title: Hands-on: weighted averages
steps: Make one group of 2 values averaging 10 and another of 3 averaging 20.
experiment.result: The combined mean is 80/5=16, not 15.

lessons.title: Stacked and 100-percent bars
ideas: A stacked bar shows the total and its component parts.
A100-percent stacked bar shows composition, not absolute size.
Compare counts using a common scale and compare percentages with stated totals.

examples.question: In class A ($30$ pupils) $40\%$ play chess; in class B ($50$ pupils) $30\%$ do. Which has more chess players?
examples.result: Class B, though its percentage is lower

examples.question: A stacked bar shows $12$ walk, $20$ bus, $8$ car. Find the percentages.
Why must two pie charts show totals before comparing sector sizes?
steps: Equal sectors mean equal fractions, not equal counts.

experiment.title: Hands-on: stacked and 100-percent bars
steps: Draw bars for groups of 10 and 20, each with half in category A.
experiment.result: The composition is equal even though the second A count is twice as large.

ideas: Read the question twice and decide which idea it tests.
Write each step with a reason; check the answer in the original question.
These questions mix ideas from the whole chapter.

examples.question: The mean of $10$ observations is $25$. One value $40$ is replaced by $10$. Find the new mean.

g9-probability.subtitle: CBSE Mathematics 2026–27 · Start from basics; build confidence one step at a time

sheet.title: Outcomes, events and equally likely cases
items: P(E)=\frac{\text{favourable equally likely outcomes}}{\text{total equally likely outcomes}}

lessons.title: Outcomes, events and equally likely cases
ideas: A sample space lists possible outcomes.
An event is a collection of outcomes.
Counting favourable outcomes works directly only when the listed outcomes are equally likely.
formulas: P(E)=\frac{\text{favourable equally likely outcomes}}{\text{total equally likely outcomes}}

examples.question: A card is drawn from cards numbered $1$ to $20$. Find P(prime).
A letter is chosen from the word PROBABILITY. Find P(B).
A bag has $4$ red, $5$ green and $6$ yellow balls. Find P(not green).

experiment.title: Hands-on: outcomes, events and equally likely cases
steps: List the faces of a fair die.
experiment.result: Three of six equally likely cases gives probability one half.

lessons.title: Experimental probability
ideas: Relative frequency is an experimental estimate, not an exact prediction.
More trials often stabilise an estimate but do not guarantee any exact next outcome.
A fair coin can produce uneven short runs.

examples.question: A die is thrown $60$ times and shows $6$ eleven times. Find the experimental probability of a $6$.
$200$ bulbs are tested; $12$ are faulty. Estimate how many are faulty in a box of $1000$.
A coin gave $7$ heads in $10$ tosses. Is it unfair?
steps: A short run can differ from $\tfrac12$ by chance.

experiment.title: Hands-on: experimental probability
steps: Toss a coin 20 times and record heads.
Compare your fraction with one half.
experiment.result: A difference does not itself prove the coin unfair.

lessons.title: Use tables and trees
ideas: For two ordered coin tosses, HH,HT,TH,TT are distinct equally likely outcomes.
Tree branches organise multi-step possibilities.
State replacement and independence before multiplying branch probabilities.

examples.question: Two fair coins are tossed. Using the tree shown, find P(two tails) and P(at most one head).
steps: Two tails: $1$ leaf. At most one head: $3$ leaves.

examples.question: Two dice are thrown. Find P(doublet) and P(sum $10$).
A bag has $4$ red and $1$ blue ball. Two are drawn with replacement. Find P(both red).

experiment.title: Hands-on: use tables and trees
steps: Draw two branches H,T for the first fair toss.
Split each again for the second toss.
experiment.result: Four leaves show why one head can occur in two different orders.

diagram.caption: A tree for two independent tosses of a fair coin.

lessons.title: Complements and careful interpretation
ideas: A probability lies from 0 to 1.
A complementary event contains every outcome outside the event.
Probability zero means impossible in a finite equally likely model, not merely unlikely.

examples.question: If P(rain) $=0.35$, find P(no rain).
Can $\tfrac76$ be a probability? Can $-0.2$?
A die is thrown. Find P(number less than $7$) and P(number $7$).
steps: Every outcome is less than $7$; none is $7$.

experiment.title: Hands-on: complements and careful interpretation
steps: Circle the remaining outcomes as the complement.
experiment.result: The two groups together use all six outcomes with no overlap.
